newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech govt to raise drug prices after crown fall.
newsitem.headline: Czech govt to raise drug prices after crown fall.

text.p: The Czech Finance Ministry said on Thursday it would amend its maximum price list for pharmaceuticals, partially incorporating exchange rate losses of medicine importers due to a fall of the crown.

Local subsidiaries of major foreign drug producers have called for an increase of the maximum prices or total deregulation, saying they might be forced to keep some of their drugs off the Czech market due to the currency's recent drop.

Deputy Finance Minister Jana Fuerstova told Reuters that the new price list, which will be valid from July, would set price increases based on inflation in the countries of origin and changes of the crown's exchange rate with currencies of those countries.
"We adjusted the proposals of the prices according to these two criteria. To a certain extent we reflected the (crown) devaluation hit," she told Reuters,
She declined to reveal details of the planned changes.
The Czech crown plummeted after speculative attacks forced the central bank to float the currency and abandon its 15 percent fluctuation band on May 27.
The currency has lost about 15 percent from its peak in February, and about nine percent against the dollar and 6.5 percent against the mark after the currency was floated.
The International Association of Pharmaceutical Companies (MASF), which includes major Czech importers, said before Fuerstova's statement that some vital drugs could be pushed away from the market.
In a statement it also called for "negotiations for preparing and implementing more tranparent rules" for pricing and "serious debate on price deregulation".

"Generally, MAFS members have not increased prices of their products during the last five years and, with a few exceptions, the prices of our products on the market are lower compared to prices on markets in countries of their origin," the statement said.
The deputy minister said that compensation for the drop of the currency would not be complete.

"There are exchange rate risks aready incorporated in the calculations (importers' proposals for price increases) done in January. We made the adjustments according to our internal rules, which apply to everybody in the same way," she said.

Fuerstova said many of the importers' threats to leave the market were unfounded, but added that her office and the health ministry were ready to negotiate separate cases if there was a danger of a suspension of supplies of an unsubstitutable, vital drug.
Fuerstova said that there were enough drugs on the market at the moment, and that her department would analyse further developments and make changes to the regulations in October if necessary.
